newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK & Shanghai Hotels sees strong growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: HK & Shanghai Hotels sees strong growth in 1997.

text.p: Luxury hotel and property concern Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels Ltd should achieve good earnings growth in 1997, senior executives said in conjunction with the release of the company's 1996 results on Wednesday.
"We are looking for good growth in 1997," Douglas Webster, director of financial and corporate services, told a news conference.
The growth will come from the positive outlook for the hotel industry in Hong Kong and the United States this year and from new acquisitions, company executives said.
The company announced profit after tax and minority interests of HK$861 million for the year to December 31, 1996, an increase of 32 percent compared with HK$652 million in 1995.
Earnings per share were HK$0.79 compared with HK$0.60 in 1995, an increase of 32 percent.
The profit figure excluded the HK$55 million extraordinary gain on the sale of the group's 25 percent stake in Cathay Pacific Catering Services (HK) Ltd, sold in March 1996.
Total profit attributable to shareholders rose to HK$916 million, a 40 percent increase over 1995.
The results included an exceptional loss of HK$95 million.
"This represents an addition to the provisions which we have made against the carrying value of our projects in Thailand," said Webster. "In 1997, we shall review the position again."
The group made similar provisions of HK$70 million in 1994 and HK$80 million in 1995.
The Hong Kong Society of Accountants' change to the accounting standards several years ago drastically limited the items which could be considered extraordinary, said Webster.

"Our directors consider that this limitation leads to information which is misleading to shareholders and investors and to the public and therefore we continued to deal with items which are not part of our core business as extraordinary and therefore received qualification from the auditors," he said.
Looking ahead, the company should achieve good growth in earnings in 1997.
"The hotel industry in Hong Kong will be very strong in 1997," said Pierre Boppe, chief executive officer.

Boppe said Hong Kong would host three major events -- the World Cup Rugby Sevens in March, the handover of the British territory to Chinese rule at the end of June and the joint World Bank-International Monetary Fund conference in September.

Chairman Michael Kadoorie said the company's earnings base would expand following the acquisition this month of Quail Lodge Inc, comprising Quail Lodge, a 100-room resort hotel with golf course in Carmel Valley, California, and the Quail Meadows residential development with 32 housing lots for sale.
The company hoped to open its much-delayed Peninsula Bangkok hotel in the first half of 1998, Kadoorie said.
"I would expect that in the end if we achieve a goal of, say, 12 Peninsula hotels around the world, we will have done extremely well," Kadoorie said.
The group has four wholly owned hotels and holds equity positions in hotels in Beijing, Manila and Los Angeles, in addition to its Bangkok and Jakarta projects.
The group also owns upmarket residential and commercial property in Hong Kong, New York and Ho Chi Minh City.
Kadoorie would not discuss the company's Sydney residential and hotel complex to be located near the city's famous opera house, which has drawn opposition from local groups.
"Our aim for Sydney is to have the hotel ready for the Olympics in the year 2000, but it is a little too early to bring it in (for discussion)," Kadoorie said.
